reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: Typically presents as sudden, painless, unilateral loss or blurring of vision, most often in older patients with vascular risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes, or hyperviscosity
Fundus shows the classic 'blood and thunder' picture: widespread retinal haemorrhages in all four quadrants, dilated tortuous veins, cotton-wool spots, and optic disc swelling
Clinically divided into non-ischaemic (perfused) and ischaemic (non-perfused) types, with the ischaemic form carrying much higher risk of neovascular complications
A relative afferent pupillary defect and poor initial visual acuity are markers of an ischaemic occlusion
The most feared complication is neovascular ('90-day') glaucoma from rubeosis iridis; the eye must be monitored for iris and angle new vessels
Macular oedema is the main cause of reduced central vision and is managed with intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy or intravitreal steroid
Ischaemic retina and neovascularisation are treated with pan-retinal photocoagulation to reduce the angiogenic drive
A younger patient with CRVO warrants evaluation for thrombophilia, inflammatory, and hyperviscosity causes
reference.pathophysiology: Central retinal vein occlusion results from thrombosis of the central retinal vein at or posterior to the lamina cribrosa, where the central retinal artery and vein share a common adventitial sheath; arteriosclerotic thickening of the artery compresses the vein and promotes turbulent flow and thrombus formation. The resulting rise in venous and capillary pressure causes widespread retinal haemorrhage, oedema, and, when perfusion fails, capillary non-perfusion and retinal ischaemia. Ischaemic retina releases vascular endothelial growth factor, driving macular oedema and neovascularisation of the retina, optic disc, and iris, which can lead to neovascular glaucoma.
additionalDifferentials: Papilloedema or anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy
additionalInvestigations: Dilated fundus examination to assess haemorrhage distribution, ischaemia, and disc swelling
Optical coherence tomography to detect and quantify macular oedema
Fluorescein angiography to distinguish ischaemic from non-ischaemic disease and map capillary non-perfusion
Intraocular pressure measurement and gonioscopy to detect angle neovascularisation
Blood pressure, blood glucose, and lipid assessment; thrombophilia and inflammatory screen in younger patients
redFlags: New iris or angle vessels (rubeosis) or a rising intraocular pressure heralding neovascular glaucoma
Relative afferent pupillary defect with poor acuity indicating an ischaemic occlusion
Rapidly worsening vision or pain suggesting progression to neovascular glaucoma
Bilateral or young-patient presentation suggesting a systemic hyperviscosity or thrombophilic disorder
reference.prognosis: Non-ischaemic CRVO often has a reasonable visual outcome, though some cases convert to the ischaemic form over time. Ischaemic CRVO carries a poor visual prognosis and a high risk of neovascular glaucoma; timely anti-VEGF therapy for macular oedema and laser for ischaemia improve outcomes but vision is frequently limited.
pitfalls: Assuming a good early prognosis without follow-up, missing conversion from non-ischaemic to ischaemic disease
Failing to examine the iris and angle for neovascularisation at each review
Overlooking treatable systemic risk factors such as uncontrolled hypertension
Not considering a hyperviscosity or thrombophilic cause in younger or bilateral cases
management: Intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy as the mainstay for macular oedema, with intravitreal corticosteroid as an alternative
Panretinal photocoagulation laser for ischaemic disease and retinal or disc neovascularisation
Regular monitoring for anterior segment neovascularisation and neovascular glaucoma with gonioscopy and intraocular pressure checks, treating rubeosis iridis promptly
Management of intraocular pressure and neovascular glaucoma when it develops
Identification and control of systemic risk factors including hypertension, diabetes and hyperlipidaemia, with a thrombophilia and inflammatory screen in younger patients
Optical coherence tomography and fluorescein angiography to monitor oedema and distinguish the ischaemic type
